objects: dense SNP mapping; causal variants; candidate genes
assumptions: GWAS-associated regions contain multiple candidate SNPs
conclusion: Fine mapping seeks to identify candidate genes and causal variants and exclude regions and SNPs unlikely to be causal.
scope: Motivation for dense follow-up genotyping of GWAS-associated regions.
span: This follow-up genotyping, often referred to as fine mapping, can identify new candidate genes and causal variants in GWAS-identified regions, for example, the nonsynonymous SNP rs3184504 in SH2B3 in type 1 diabetes4. In addition, it can lead to the identification of regions and SNPs that are highly unlikely to be causal.

objects: SNP genotype configurations in disease cases and controls
conclusion: The Bayesian association analysis uses the genotype configuration at each SNP in cases and controls.
scope: Individual-level case-control genotypes; the main manuscript does not specify a summary-statistic-only implementation.
span: We adopted a Bayesian statistical perspective for analysis, with the strength of evidence for association measured via the Bayes factor for each SNP: the probability of the genotype configuration at that SNP in cases and controls under the alternative hypothesis that the SNP is associated with disease status divided by the probability of the genotype configuration at that SNP in cases and controls under the null hypothesis that disease status is independent of genotype at that SNP (Supplementary Note).

objects: BF_k; posterior probability for SNP k; sum of regional Bayes factors
assumptions: exactly one genotyped SNP is causal; equal prior probability across genotyped SNPs
conclusion: The regional posterior probability for SNP k is computed by dividing its Bayes factor by the sum of the Bayes factors for all SNPs in the region.
scope: Closed-form normalization conditional on Bayes factors; their detailed computation is deferred to the Supplementary Note.
span: Defining BFk as the Bayes factor for SNP k, we show in the Supplementary Note that the posterior probably for SNP k is equal to (BF_{k})/(∑ j BF_{j}) where j indexes SNPs in the region.

objects: regional SNP posterior probabilities; 95% and 99% credible sets

conclusion: A regional credible set is the smallest set of SNPs accounting for the chosen 95% or 99% posterior probability.
scope: Posterior uncertainty about causal identity within the analyzed region.
span: Uncertainty after fine mapping as to the identity of the causal SNPs is conveniently handled by describing credible sets. In each region, one can choose the smallest set of SNPs accounting for 95% or 99% of the posterior probability.

conclusion: The authors state informally that, when the true causal SNP has been genotyped, one can be reasonably confident it lies in the relevant credible set.
scope: Informal author-stated interpretation; the main manuscript gives no repeated-sampling coverage theorem.
span: These credible sets are somewhat analogous to confidence intervals: in a particular region, if the true causal SNP has been genotyped, we can be reasonably confident that it will be in the relevant credible set.

objects: posterior probabilities; single typed causal SNP; allelic heterogeneity
assumptions: some studied regions violate the single typed causal SNP assumption
conclusion: The calculated posterior probabilities depend on a single causal SNP being typed, and the authors state that this assumption fails in some studied regions.
scope: Validity of the causal-probability interpretation when the assumed causal configuration is wrong.
span: The calculated value of the posterior probability depends on a number of assumptions, including the assumption that there is a single causal SNP that is typed in the study. This will not always be the case, and, indeed, our data show this is not true for several of the regions we studied, most notably CDKN2A-CDKN2B in T2D (Supplementary Note).

objects: effect size; sample size; extended strong linkage disequilibrium
assumptions: small effects; very strong and extended linkage disequilibrium
conclusion: Smaller effects require much larger samples, and very large samples can still be uninformative when linkage disequilibrium is very strong and extended.
scope: Qualitative author-stated limitation of fine-mapping resolution; no quantitative sample-size bound is stated.
span: For smaller effect sizes, much larger sample sets are required, and, even then, if linkage disequilibrium is very strong and extended, very large sample sizes can still be uninformative.

objects: pairwise posterior-probability ratio; pairwise Bayes-factor ratio
assumptions: posterior probabilities calculated using the stated equal-prior regional normalization
conclusion: The ratio of the calculated posterior probabilities for two SNPs equals their Bayes-factor ratio, which summarizes their relative evidence.
scope: Identity for the calculated weights; the discussion uses it to interpret evidence even when causal-model assumptions fail.
span: Nonetheless, the ratio of these posterior probabilities for a pair of SNPs reduces to the ratio of the Bayes factors for the pair, and, in a Bayesian framework, this ratio is the quantity that summarizes the weight of evidence in the data for one SNP compared to the other (as shown, for example, in Table 2).

scope: Qualitative author assertion without a formal error bound or robustness theorem in the main manuscript.
span: Regardless of whether the causal SNP or SNPs have been typed in the fine-mapping experiment, SNPs with a low value for this posterior probability are unlikely to be causal.
